Owner Passed Before Finishing This 1961 Ford, the Mileage Is Unexpected
26 photos
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25
The previous owner passed before finishing. This is how the current owner of this 1961 Ford Thunderbird describes the car, revealing that it’s a work in progress that has every part it needs in the trunk.
In other words, this 1961 Thunderbird is exactly what you need if you want an easy project. The car is already complete, so theoretically, someone with the right skills only needs to put it back together and bring the car to the road.
It’s not an easy project, though. It’s all because this T-Bird deserves the touch of a professional, especially as it seems to check all the boxes for a collectible.
First, it looks original. Second, it appears to be complete. Third, it has a fantastic number on the clock. Fourth, despite being described as a barn find, it’s running and driving.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 Not many people remember this, but a Thunderbird convertible was chosen in 1961 to pace the Indianapolis 500. This helped the T-Bird gain more popularity, and this was more than welcome, especially considering the prices. It didn’t take long for the base Thunderbird to cost more than $5,000, so Ford had no option but to convince buyers that the car was worth the price.
“Here is the finest expression of the Thunderbird spirit, unquestionably Thunderbird in its classic lines and sparkling performance - not a hair wider nor a tenth of an inch longer - yet a Thunderbird so uniquely new that it stands alone in the fine-car field,” Ford said.
Ford used its booklets and marketing materials mostly to highlight the premium features on the T-Bird. One of them was the Swing-Away Steering Wheel.
“The steering wheel moves over to welcome you in,” Ford explained, revealing that the steering wheel could be moved for up to 10 inches to “take the driver’s seat easily.”
The Thunderbird was fitted with a 390 Special V8 paired with a new Cruise-O-Matic transmission, power steering, and power brakes. All these goodies were offered standard on every T-Bird sold this year.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 That’s why this Ford Thunderbird should return to the road. It looks mostly original, and the engine under the hood is a correct 390. Unfortunately, the seller doesn’t share more specifics about the powertrain, but considering it’s a barn find that’s been sitting for quite a while, I would assume that it’s the original unit.
A quick inspection and a verification of the numbers should help any potential buyer figure out the whole story, so just call the seller and ask for additional data.
It’s unclear if the engine has already been rebuilt, but it starts and runs. It needs carb work, the seller reveals, so my recommendation is that you ask your mechanic to go there in person and see what they find under the hood.
The car also needs a brake booster, but a new one is in the trunk, along with all the other extras that might appear to be missing when you inspect the car digitally.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 The metal looks fairly solid, which makes me think that the previous owner who started working on this Thunderbird was focused mostly on the metalwork. I would still check everything in person before making an offer, especially if the long-term objective is keeping this T-Bird original and returning it to the day-one configuration.
Look for patches under the car because a long time of sitting typically means that the floors are struggling with the invasion of rust. It’s unclear if the undersides have already been fixed or they didn’t require much work, but that’s what live inspections are for.
1961 Thunderbirds aren’t necessarily rare, so I think that the main selling point for this specimen is the number on the clock and how complete it continues to be after all these years. The odometer shows a little over 29K miles, and it’s safe to assume that this is the original mileage. However, I would still have this checked, especially if the goal is a complete restoration.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 As for the price, I don’t think it’s necessarily ambitious, but considering 1961 Thunderbirds aren’t the most desirable, it looks like the car will have a hard time finding a new home.
The owner listed the car for auction, with the starting bid set at $5,000. A reserve is also in place, meaning that while you’ll have to bid $5,000 to join the digital fight, you’ll have to pay more to win it. I believe the reserve’s value is close to the BIN price, which is $7,000 for this auction.
Unsurprisingly, the auction is still at 0 bids, and there’s a chance the price is keeping people away for the time being. I still expect the car to sell eventually, but a no-reserve auction would have increased its chances to find a buyer on the first attempt.
The car is parked in Walnut, Grove, Missouri, and the auction is scheduled to end in 6 days.
